Disease Outbreak Hits Argentine Fisheries Industry, Forcing Plant Closures and Worker Absences

BUENOS AIRES, June 14 – An outbreak of norovirus has disrupted operations at several fisheries plants along Argentina’s Patagonian coast, industry officials said Friday, as companies scramble to contain the spread among workers and maintain output during the peak winter fishing season.

The outbreak, first detected last week at a processing facility in Puerto Madryn, has since spread to at least five other sites in Chubut and Santa Cruz provinces, affecting over 350 workers, according to the National Fisheries Chamber. The highly contagious virus, which causes acute gastroenteritis, has led to mass absences and prompted the temporary shutdown of several processing lines.

“Production has slowed significantly in the last ten days,” said Marta Ledesma, director of the Fisheries Workers’ Union. “We have more than 200 workers on medical leave in just two plants, and others are working with reduced shifts.” She added that companies are implementing enhanced sanitation protocols and screening measures, but warned that further spread could force additional closures.

The affected companies include Mar Austral S.A. and Pesca Patagónica S.R.L., both major employers in the region. A spokesperson for Mar Austral said, “We are prioritizing the health of our staff and following all guidelines from health authorities. Our Puerto Deseado plant is operating at 40% capacity due to staff shortages.”

Industry analysts estimate daily processing volumes for hake and squid are down by roughly 30% since the outbreak began, with delays in filleting and packaging. “This is an industry that relies heavily on seasonal labor and fast turnaround,” said analyst Gabriel Mansilla. “Even a short-term disruption can have lasting impacts on inventory and export schedules.”

The Fisheries Secretariat said it is monitoring the situation and coordinating with public health officials to support affected plants. “Our main concern is worker safety and preventing further transmission,” said Secretariat spokesperson Lucía Ramírez.

Union officials called for expanded on-site medical support and sick pay guarantees for infected workers. “We urge companies to act swiftly to protect both workers and the industry’s long-term stability,” said Ledesma.

The outbreak remains ongoing, with further updates expected as health investigations continue.
